In a series of X posts, he called Belfast’s mayor a “betrayer of her people” and a British political leader a “scumbag and a traitor.” For years, Musk has used his social-media megaphone to boost antiestablishment parties outside the U.S. But no foreign nation has drawn such sustained attention from the world’s richest man as the U.K., according to a Journal investigation. Musk’s effort to reshape Britain has caused political turmoil , leaving government ministers at a loss over how to push back without provoking a direct confrontation with the Trump administration, report Jenny Strasburg, Jaclyn Jeffrey-Wilensky and Max Colchester.

Mandatory FAA medical exams can ground them long before the required retirement age of 65. They earn more than four times the average worker—the most seasoned pilots earn far more—but they have little control over the management of the company they have wedded themselves to.

Surging Energy Costs Split Companies Over Whether to Raise Prices Now
 
Plus, Elon Musk trains his political chaos machine on the U.K., and what we’re watching for at the biggest Fed meeting of the year
 
 
JUSTIN SULLIVAN/GETTY IMAGES
 

1. FROM MY DESK

 

Business owners face a thorny question: Are high energy costs a temporary nuisance, or an entrenched reality that calls for price hikes right now? The answers have important implications for the U.S. economy.

 

As the Federal Reserve weighs an interest-rate rise today, businesses are pulling their own economic levers. Some are holding their ground, betting price shocks will recede. Others believe energy and trade volatility are here to stay, leaving zero wiggle room to absorb the hit.

 

We spoke to farmers, manufacturers and economists to see how companies are navigating the pricing maze—and what consumers can expect at checkout.

 

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here. If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.

 
 
 

2. TODAY’S HEADLINES

 

• European Union chief Ursula von der Leyen proposed making Canada the first associate member of the bloc.

 

• The U.S. is burning through its supply of interceptors to counter Iran’s attacks.

 

• The Pentagon wants only the fittest troops to attend Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s “State of the Force” address.

 

• Charlie Kirk’s widow Erika Kirk said in a legal claim that Utah Valley University failed to protect him, notifying officials that she may take legal action against the university and the state.

 

• European fintech firm Revolut gave hundreds of its customers’ data to someone masquerading as a government agency—and the customers are angry.

 

• Some of China’s scrappiest hackers-for-hire are evolving into full-service private intelligence agencies.

A bill the industry had long been lobbying for failed to clear a procedural vote in the U.S. Senate. (Get Spencer’s Markets A.M. newsletter in your inbox.)

 

• OpenAI has held early discussions with investors about a new funding round that could value it at more than $1.2 trillion.

 

• With the FDA’s hard-liners gone, this corner of biotech is back in favor, writes David Wainer.

 
 
 

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

 

Elon Musk trains his political chaos machine on the U.K.

 

On the eve of becoming the world’s first trillionaire, Elon Musk was fixated on political turmoil an ocean away. In a series of X posts, he called Belfast’s mayor a “betrayer of her people” and a British political leader a “scumbag and a traitor.” For years, Musk has used his social-media megaphone to boost antiestablishment parties outside the U.S. But no foreign nation has drawn such sustained attention from the world’s richest man as the U.K., according to a Journal investigation. Musk’s effort to reshape Britain has caused political turmoil, leaving government ministers at a loss over how to push back without provoking a direct confrontation with the Trump administration, report Jenny Strasburg, Jaclyn Jeffrey-Wilensky and Max Colchester.

 

5.

 

Airline pilots are America’s most unpredictable millionaires.

 

Many pilots leave the workforce as millionaires thanks to generous pay and 401(k) contributions from their employers. But they face lots of pitfalls, too, reports Miriam Gottfried. They typically work for the same carrier their entire careers, and in a volatile industry working for the wrong airline at the wrong time can take a toll on earnings. Mandatory FAA medical exams can ground them long before the required retirement age of 65. They earn more than four times the average worker—the most seasoned pilots earn far more—but they have little control over the management of the company they have wedded themselves to.

 

• While we’re in the air: Getting your seat downgraded on a flight is becoming more common. Our travel columnist explains how to press your case.

6. SEE THE STORY

Some 75% of trans-Atlantic cables run through Irish waters, but the historically neutral country presents a possible weak link in the West’s defenses. Correspondent Sune Engel Rasmussen joined the country’s navy on a recent patrol of the Irish Sea.

 
 
 

7. HAPPENING TODAY

 

• The Fed concludes its two-day policy meeting with a rate decision. Our chief economics correspondent Nick Timiraos outlines the top three issues he’s watching for.

 

• WSJ live Q&A: Do you have questions about the new iPhone Duo, iOS 27, or the new Siri? Join our personal tech columnist Nicole Nguyen for a Q&A session at 1 p.m. ET.

 

• Economic data: The Commerce Department releases August retail-sales figures.

 

• 📰 Today’s paper

 
 
 

8. THE NUMBER

 
$107 billion
 

That’s roughly how much extra U.S. consumers have spent on gasoline and diesel during the Iran conflict and disruptions from the Russia-Ukraine conflict, according to estimates by the Climate Solutions Lab at Brown University. Higher pump prices have led many families to save less and curb spending elsewhere.

 
 
 

9. AND FINALLY…

 

Nothing blows up a parent group like a fight over school snacks.

 

By now, much of the internet has heard of Oreo-gate: a viral social-media saga in which a kindergarten mother asks other moms in a group chat to stop sending Oreos in their children’s lunches because it was making her daughter jealous. The drama escalated quickly. Screenshots of the exchange racked up millions of views on Instagram. The posts turned out to be fictional, but parents and teachers say the warfare over school snacks is very real.
